catalog_quote: Kisi is a tonal language with the following tones: Low, High, Extra-High (limited distribution), Rise, and Fall. Tone is used lexically with nouns and grammatically elsewhere, especially within the verbal morphology. [Abstract, p. 1] || The most important feature of Kisi's suprasegmental inventory is the use of tone to signal lexical and grammatical differences. [...] The tonal system of Kisi has two level tones and two contour tones, which are transparently derived from level tones in some cases. Furthermore, the high tone is the "marked" tone, as is the case with the majority of tonal systems. [...] An unusual, but not unknown, feature is the extra-high tone of Kisi. It is used sparingly in the language, functioning in only a few grammatical contexts. Another suprasegmental feature found in Kisi is contrastive vowel length for all (non-diphthongized) vowels. [p. 22] || The extra-high tone is higher in frequency (155 Hz vs 144 Hz), louder (82.9 dB vs 80.0 db), and longer (199 vs 193 msec) than the regular high tone (all perceptible differences), and informants insist on a distinction between the two (Childs 1988a). [pp. 73-74]
world_status: statement found in an open source

"The tonal system of K…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kisi is a tone language (two level tones H/L, two contour tones R/F, plus a grammatically restricted extra-high tone); the only full phonological description that is openly accessible makes no statement about word stress at all — the word 'stress' occurs only for English source words (p. 92: 'high tones are found on stressed syllables of borrowed English words'). No stress position can be coded; the record is 'tonal, no stress statement'.
new_statements.exceptions: The extra-high tone (Negative Perfective/Habitual verbs, some ideophones) is measured as higher (155 vs 144 Hz), louder (82.9 vs 80.0 dB) and longer (199 vs 193 ms) than plain High (pp. 73-74), and Childs' companion paper (1988a/1989, not obtained) asks whether it is 'a new system of prominence'; p. 110 treats verbs as 'accentual' in an autosegmental sense (Low-toned verb syllables are 'non-accented' and receive a floating High). Ideophones show exaggerated pitch register (JALL 1988: 177). None of this is a word-stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: lexical tone on nouns and other classes, grammatical tone melodies on verbs (e.g. Past = LH assigned left-to-right by syllable, pp. 82-83); utterance level: downdrift and a final fall, WH-question rise-fall tune (sec. 3.4 Intonation, pp. 86-91). Citation forms not separately discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Childs (1988) describes the Kisi of Sierra Leone/Liberia/Guinea as one language; his fieldwork variety is the southern (Sierra Leone/Liberia) Kisi = ISO kss = sout2778 (the dissertation p. 8 area notes speakers 'from French Guinea had a different accent'). Northern Kissi (kqs, nort2765) is a separate Glottolog languoid and is not covered by any file here.

sources.note: Silent on word stress in Kisi ('stress' appears only for English: aspiration 'before stressed vowels' p. 46, and 'high tones are found on stressed syllables of borrowed English words' p. 92). Describes Kisi as tonal: H, L, Rise, Fall + restricted extra-high (abstract; p. 22; sec. 3.3.1 pp. 66-74); extra-high is higher/louder/longer than H (pp. 73-74); verbs 'accentual' in autosegmental sense (p. 110).
Bibliographic only; alternative names Gisi, Gissi, Gizi, Kissi, Kissien.

sources.note: No stress statement. p. 171: 'There are four basic tones in Kisi, with an extra-high tone of limited distribution. There are two level tones: a High tone and a Low tone; and two contour tones: a Rising tone, and a Falling tone. The Extra-High tone.. is found only in the verbal morphology. Tone is both grammatical (verbs, syntactic constructions) and lexical (all other word classes).' p. 177: ideophones carry an exaggerated pitch register / extra-high over the whole word. (PDXScholar ling_fac/4 is an automated-access block-challenged; copy taken archived copy (Internet Archive, 21 Jul 2024).)
Second-hand: 'Kissi has four tones: two register and two contour.. an extra-high tone occurs only sparingly'; no mention of stress.
